questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, KU Leuven had introductory seminaries on living in Leuven, registereing etc.

questions.answer: Introduction to living in Leuven

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: KU Leuven has a range of dorms, which students can apply for. I lived at the Leo XIII Seminary.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: We had a weekly common dinner in my dorm community. We had access to a kitchen, though I do not recommend making use of such facilities, as they were very unsanitary.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I'd recommend getting an apartment instead. The university dorms are not in good shape, and unfortunately, some of the residents don't clean up after themselves leaving common areas very dirty, unsanitary and even rat-infested.

Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We signed up for classes via an online tool. THere is a small period before you have to finalize your academic programme, giving the opportunity to get a feeling for classes before committing. It can be difficult to make it all work, as there are many small courses you'll have to take, and a lot of them may overlap.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Exchange coordinators.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Mostly succesful, though I had to make some compromises due to scheduling.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It's not a vacation. Prior to leaving I had heard from students of other destinations that exchange was easier than Denmark. I found this not to be the case at KU Leuven. The workload is high and the threshold for suceeding is also high. You will need to dedicate time to studying and learning. But you'll also get to know many fields of law, engage with some of the brightest legal minds europe has to offer, and hone your legal skills and perspective.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found the classes to be a bit more difficult than in Denmark. Though, comparison is tough, as classes are between 3-6 ECTS points which 'on paper' is smaller than in Denmark, though, the workload of the courses were higher than I expected. I generally found KU Leuven to be more difficult than UCPH, but not to an unreasonable extent.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: More lecture based. Professors will engage in discussions, but the classes are big. This does mean that you'll be taught by the head of courses.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.answer:

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Judicial Protection in the European Union - Provides great insight into procedure at the CJEU, which i found to be very interesting.
Labour Policy and Law - Part of the exam is a paper, which you have to write with other students, comparing your national legislations. Provides great international perspective.
European Company Law - Very interesting course. Professor Marieke Wyckaert is one of the most brilliant, kind and caring persons I've ever met. I am truly fortunate to have learned from her.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can get a sports card. I played a lot of sports, there's a whole sports campus, so you can entertain your newfound friends with your skills in football, padel, volleyball, spikeball and so on!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you like drinking - go to a cantus. I'd also recommend going to see Brugge (Bruges), which I thought was very beautiful.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Take the train to other Belgian cities, or even outside of Belgium. You are close to many great cities.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Socially it was easy. But I never adjusted to the way the treat common facilities at dorms.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The only up side of living at a dorm is that it's very easy to encounter and get to know the nationals. Outside of the dorm community Belgians can be reserved, and may not be very interested in exchange students - so I've been told. Personally I only experienced people being kind and welcoming, and I mostly just tried being myself. Learning a few words or sentences may help you along the way, showing interest in their culture in general is a good way to engage.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Cleanliness in common facilities.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The academic environment.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Sign up for a local health insurance fund (its free) - CM was my choice
Make an honest commitment to learning and studying
Go for walks - It's a very walkable city with a lot of gems you'll randomly encounter on a good walk

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: N/A

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The newly gained international perspective

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: My greatest challenge was food, as the kitchen was rat-infested and no one cared. I didn't wanna cook food in a rat-infested kitchen, so I had to eat most of my meals at the school canteen (it's called alma), which didn't really align with my dietary preferences.

questions.question: Any other comments?

questions.answer: Yes
